name: Lena Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. Tell me how an ordinary day goes at your accounting firm.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The ferry operator sends a ticket file and a separate list of refunds, and I match them before preparing its accounts and tax return for a senior to review. I like spotting one duplicated crossing before it becomes a larger tax error; the dull part is copying the same ticket number into two forms. I am 58, with a bachelor's degree in accounting, and I am still a junior learning the work. I use AI every day to sort a draft exception list, then check each flagged fare against the booking record myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI mostly stays where it is, my exception list is still useful but does not close the ferry return for me. The refund record needs a person to check it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team to keep the booking record behind every correction. I would tell the operator which crossing was counted twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pay is about typical for an accountant, and my partner Owen and I have around three months of expenses saved. Our grown son has his own household, we cover our regular home costs while both working, and there are some accounting firms nearby if a real vacancy appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep preparing the paid ferry accounts and checking the approved AI exception list against bookings. I would ask my manager Imani to remove one duplicate ticket-entry step only after a paid test on old files matches the signed totals and she approves the live change in writing; otherwise I would keep the current process.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this limited change, though I still want to know what our later income will be. The duplicate entry is a nuisance, not a reason to gamble on a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is your test file?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use a closed month with the known refunded crossings marked. If the tool leaves one fare in twice, it does not pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your son work with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He has his own work and home. I might show him a funny ticket error, but I would not count his wage in our plans.

I would explain the **duplicated crossing** to the operator.
think: Our **three-month reserve** and two current wages keep bills manageable.
Some nearby firms provide **options** only when an actual opening exists.
do: Keep **paid ferry accounts** and check approved AI exception lists against bookings.
Remove a **duplicate ticket entry** only after paid old-file proof and Imani's written approval; otherwise retain the process.
feel: I feel **calm** about a limited tool change.
S0.quote: The duplicate entry is a nuisance, not a reason to gamble on a new job.
fieldNote: She uses AI **daily** but checks every flagged fare against source bookings before a senior signs the return.
The process change needs **paid old-file proof** and Imani's written live approval, preserving current work if the test fails.

steps.text: Keep paid ferry returns and check approved exception lists against bookings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The writing and checking on the card could include much of my ferry file. Robots may later handle physical port work, but the desk would change first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the firm to count wrong fare matches before shortening anyone's hours. I would tell the operator not to trust a neat AI draft without the booking behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own junior hours could be reduced if the senior gets faster drafts and needs fewer helpers. Three months saved gives us some room, but Owen's maintenance wage alone would not cover all our household bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Imani for a paid two-week test of the new ferry-refund checker against anonymised signed records, only with written approval. If it passes, I would learn the approved checker on paid time and use it live only after written sign-off; if refused or failed, I would keep the present paid checks while offered. If hours fall in the first year, I would take a posted junior accounts job only with written wage, hours and start date covering our regular bills after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own hours, though I enjoy learning a tool that earns its place. The ferry cannot refund a passenger with a pretty spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which errors matter most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A ticket refunded and still counted as income matters more than a faster letter. Imani and I would sign the error count before a live file changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Owen change shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Owen's maintenance rota varies with repairs. I would check the actual rota before agreeing to new hours, not plan around a possible swap.

feel: I feel **anxious** about shorter paid weeks.

fieldNote: Daily AI experience makes her willing to test, but **signed error counts** and paid learning govern deployment.
The written job offer must cover **bills after travel** and fit Owen's actual maintenance rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 could match tickets, decide exceptions and write the tax return without my junior desk. Robots around 2031 would be later for physical port work, not an extension for these accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the firm for the date of any final paid shift and the terms on the last payslip. I would tell Owen we need to decide from the actual notice, not a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior accounting post to go when AGI does the whole fare file. Three months of cash helps, but a search could take longer, and I have woken up calculating which bills Owen's wage could carry alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would put the planned kitchen refit on hold and deposit its monthly budget into job-loss cash while my wage comes in. I would keep every paid account file offered; if my post ends in the first year after 2028, I would use the reserve for bills and seek posted ferry ticket-office shifts only with written pay, hours and start date covering our costs after travel. Ticket booking is also thinking work, so an actual paid shift would be a bridge, not safety from AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect our larger wage to go. A kitchen can wait; an empty account cannot pay for heating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the ticket office have work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know until an actual vacancy is posted. I would not leave a paid file for a conversation at the quay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Owen work more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if his employer confirms extra maintenance hours. I would not put a rumoured shift into our budget.

think: I expect my **junior accounting post** to end in 2028.
Three months saved may be shorter than a **job search**.
do: Pause the **kitchen refit** and deposit its monthly budget while wages continue.
Keep **paid account files** while offered; after loss use reserve for bills.
Take **posted ferry ticket shifts** only with written after-travel bill-covering pay, hours and start.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by expected wage loss.
S2.quote: A kitchen can wait; an empty account cannot pay for heating.
fieldNote: She separates **2028 desk AGI** from 2031 port robots, and the ticket office remains screen work exposed to AGI.
New cash comes from a **paused refit budget** while wages continue; the existing reserve funds postloss bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to find where a real person still checks ferry exceptions when AGI arrives in 2031. Robots around 2034 would later change work on the quay, not the date of our accounts shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the partners to post a paid exception-review place if the ferry operator wants one. I would tell colleagues we need a budgeted job, not a promise that quick software always needs a human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My current tax entry may shrink, but I could learn a narrower reconciliation task with supervision. I am still a junior, so I would not present myself as the operator's senior auditor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take one assigned paid ferry exception review each month with Imani checking my work, only if the operator agrees to pay the firm for it. I would keep current paid accounts; if a posted junior reconciliation role opens before or after 2031 with written wage, hours and start date covering bills after travel, I would take it. If the accounts end first, I would use the reserve for bills while looking for that actual role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the desk wage, but five years lets me see whether clients pay for a careful exception check. An unpaid pilot would tell me very little about my next income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the ferry will not pay for reviews?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would stop the extra task and keep the paid accounts files still offered. I would not let a free favour become the firm's plan for my wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for another course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn this from an assigned case with Imani, not a new certificate. If a later job requires a course, I would enrol only with employer-paid fees and paid study hours for a defined role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade brings me to 68 when AGI reaches the accounting desk in 2036. Robots around 2039 are later for physical port work, but I cannot assume my current returns last until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the firm for dated staffing plans and my retirement provider for a written estimate. I would tell Owen we should compare both with our bills before changing any hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would like a less hurried week by then, but I do not know what income would replace my wage. Three months saved is useful for a gap, not a reason to stop working without figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request a written retirement-income estimate and track six months of actual household bills, then consider a shorter paid week only if the firm confirms those hours in writing and the combined projected income covers those bills. I would keep paid ferry returns while offered; if the job ends in the first year after 2036 and income still falls short, I would use the reserve for bills and seek a posted accounts-clerk role only with written pay, hours and start date covering costs after travel. I would not decide from my age alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about a distant desk loss, but the extra years let me check the numbers carefully. I want a timetable based on the bills we have, not the bills we remember.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why track six months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our heating bill changes through the year, so one warm month lies. I want a real run of payments before reducing a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the estimate does not cover costs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid work still offered and apply only to real posted roles if it ends. Owen's maintenance pay alone may not be enough, so I would not assume retirement is funded.

I would compare them with **six months of bills** before changing hours.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the firm could stop paying for the junior fare work before a new paid role opens. Written notice, actual posted work and time to learn it on paid hours would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask how many times a passenger has paid twice before anyone spots it. I can show the same crossing on two records, and that is why I still check the booking source.

headlineQuote: I can show the same crossing on two records, and that is why I still check the booking source.
portrait: Lena is a **58-year-old junior accountant** with a bachelor's degree who learns ferry accounts through refund checks.
Her **typical pay**, three-month reserve and some nearby firms offer limited but real choice.
She uses AI **daily** but source-checks each exception and wants paid, signed tests for live changes.
She tests a **paid ferry-review task** and judges later working hours against a written income estimate and six months of bills.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** world could end her junior wage before another paid role opens.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written notice**, posted work and paid hours to learn its duties.
